brief.question: What were the main debates in the Australian parliament in 2000, and what positions did members and parties take? Debates that year included The GST arrives, The Sydney Olympics, Reconciliation and Petrol prices.
brief.answer:
The year 2000 in the Australian parliament was dominated by the implementation and political fallout of the new tax system, particularly the Goods and Services Tax (GST). The government, led by Prime Minister John Howard, championed the legislative changes as a historic achievement, citing the lowering of income taxes by $12 billion, increased family allowances of $2.4 billion, and a four per cent rise in pensions. Government speakers, including the Minister for Financial Services and Regulation, defended the scale of the reform, arguing it was the largest tax and financial reform in the nation's history and that the opposition, the Australian Labor Party (ALP), was running a "relentless negative campaign" against a tax it intended to keep.

The opposition, however, focused its attacks on the government's broken promises regarding the GST's effect on petrol prices. Labor speakers, such as the member for McEwen, accused the government of deceiving rural and regional Australia, highlighting the Prime Minister's pre-election statement that "anybody who is saying it will rise as a result of the GST is telling lies." They argued that the government's own $500 million Fuel Sales Grants Bill was a "humiliating backdown" and proof that petrol prices would rise, contrasting the original promise that prices "will not rise" with the Treasurer's later admission that they "need not rise." The opposition also moved to suspend standing orders to debate soaring petrol prices, citing the GST's cascading effect as a "tax on a tax" and accusing the government of planning a further 2 cents per litre increase in February 2001 due to excise indexation.

Beyond the GST, the government's legislative agenda included the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Bill 2000, which aimed to meet Australia's Kyoto target. While the opposition did not oppose the bill outright, reserving its right for Senate scrutiny, Labor speakers expressed concern about the government's internal tensions over climate change policy. The year also saw the government introduce the Roads to Recovery Bill 2000, which the opposition used as another platform to criticise the government's fuel policy, arguing that the broken promise on petrol prices undermined the value of additional road funding. The year concluded with the Prime Minister's valedictory speech, which celebrated the success of the Sydney Olympics and Paralympics as a source of national pride.
